meta.name: Rhetorical Mirror — Social Content Taxonomy
meta.description: A high-level classification system for detecting persuasion frameworks, narrative tropes, persuasion techniques, rhetorical devices, logical fallacies, cognitive biases, and platform or pressure tactics in posts, emails, and AI-assisted social writing.
meta.usage: Feed this taxonomy to any LLM alongside target text. The model can tag which patterns are present, estimate confidence, extract the substantive content underneath, and help rewrite a draft toward lower rhetorical density. The taxonomy is intentionally high-level rather than exhaustive.

scoring_guidance.low: Mostly direct and factual. Few visible persuasion frameworks, bias hooks, fallacies, or platform tactics.
scoring_guidance.medium: Some rhetorical packaging is present, but substance still carries the draft.
scoring_guidance.high: Persuasion frameworks, techniques, tropes, fallacies, bias hooks, or platform tactics are doing much of the persuasive work.

persuasion_frameworks.description: Foundational marketing and copywriting structures designed to move readers toward a specific action. These are the engine of the post — they shape the entire arc from opening to close.

PAS.origin: Direct-response copywriting, popularized by Dan Kennedy
PAS.mechanism: Identifies a pain point, amplifies the emotional weight of that pain, then presents the author (or their product/method) as the resolution.
detection_signals: Opens with a frustration, cost, or failure the audience recognizes
Middle section deepens the problem — consequences, wasted time/money, emotional toll
Final section pivots to a method, tool, mindset, or offer framed as the fix
The 'solve' is almost always something the author sells, teaches, or embodies
PAS.example_skeleton: 'I wasted $15K on X. Here is what nobody tells you about the real cost. After months of pain, I built a system that...'
PAS.not_this: Genuinely sharing a mistake without pivoting to self-promotion or a product

AIDA.origin: Elias St. Elmo Lewis, 1898 — the oldest documented sales funnel
AIDA.mechanism: Grabs attention with a hook, builds intellectual interest, converts interest into emotional desire, then directs toward a specific action (DM, link, subscribe).
detection_signals: Strong opening line engineered to stop the scroll
Body builds a case that makes the reader want something
Emotional or aspirational language escalates toward the end
Closes with a clear directive: DM me, grab the link, comment below
AIDA.example_skeleton: 'Most developers are mass applying and getting ignored. [Interest build-up about what works instead.] If you want my proven email template, drop TEMPLATE in the comments.'
AIDA.not_this: Sharing useful information that ends with an invitation to discuss

HSO.mechanism: Opens with an attention-grabbing hook, transitions into a relatable personal narrative that builds authority, then drops a pitch or call-to-action at the end.
detection_signals: First 1-2 lines are deliberately provocative or curiosity-inducing
Middle section tells a personal story — struggle, realization, transformation
Story conveniently leads to exactly the product/service/framework being sold
The offer may be soft ('DM me') or hard ('link in comments')
HSO.example_skeleton: 'I almost quit tech last year. [Story of burnout and recovery.] That experience is why I built [product] — grab it free this week.'
HSO.not_this: Telling a genuine story that happens to mention what you work on

narrative_tropes.description: Character archetypes and storytelling patterns the author uses to position themselves. These determine *who* the author pretends to be within the post's narrative.

PERFORMATIVE_VULNERABILITY.mechanism: Sharing a carefully curated failure or struggle, not for its own sake, but as the first act of a success story. The failure is never unresolved — it always lands on a win, a lesson, or a credential.
detection_signals: Opens with a confession of failure, rejection, or hardship
The failure is specific enough to feel authentic but sanitized of real mess
A pivot point ('but then I realized...') redirects to growth or success
The net effect is that the author looks *better* for having failed
Real vulnerability would include doubt, ambiguity, or unresolved outcomes — this doesn't
PERFORMATIVE_VULNERABILITY.example_skeleton: 'I got rejected from 47 jobs. It was the best thing that ever happened to me. Here is what I learned...'
PERFORMATIVE_VULNERABILITY.not_this: Sharing a failure that is still unresolved, still painful, or that doesn't serve the author's brand

CONTRARIAN_HUMBLEBRAG.mechanism: Disguising a flex as a controversial opinion or a reluctant admission. The author feigns hesitation or self-deprecation while ensuring the reader registers their achievement.
detection_signals: Phrases like 'unpopular opinion,' 'this might be controversial,' 'I hesitated to share this'
The 'controversial' opinion is actually safe and widely agreeable
Apparent modesty that requires the reader to infer impressive credentials
Self-deprecation that only works if the audience knows how successful the author is
CONTRARIAN_HUMBLEBRAG.example_skeleton: 'Unpopular opinion: your CS degree doesn't matter. (I say this as someone who dropped out and now leads engineering at...)'
CONTRARIAN_HUMBLEBRAG.not_this: An actually controversial opinion that risks the author's reputation

PARASOCIAL_MENTOR.mechanism: Addressing the audience as if a personal coaching relationship exists. The author positions themselves as a wise guide dispensing life advice to followers who never asked for it.
detection_signals: Direct second-person address with life advice framing: 'you need to,' 'stop doing X'
Phrases like 'here is what I would tell my younger self' or 'what I wish someone told me'
Authoritative tone without establishing why the author is qualified on this topic
Creates an implied hierarchy: author = wise mentor, reader = student
PARASOCIAL_MENTOR.example_skeleton: 'You do not need another course. You need to ship. Here are the 5 things I wish someone told me at 25...'
PARASOCIAL_MENTOR.not_this: Genuinely answering a question someone asked, or sharing expertise in context

RELUCTANT_EXPERT.mechanism: Performs modesty or hesitation before sharing advice, which makes the authority claim feel more authentic and less self-promotional.
detection_signals: Phrases like 'I do not usually share this' or 'I almost did not post this'
A modest or reluctant opening that increases trust
Hesitation framing used as a prelude to expertise or instruction
The reluctance itself becomes a credibility device
RELUCTANT_EXPERT.example_skeleton: 'I do not usually write threads like this, but after seeing the same mistake again and again, here is what I would tell founders...'
RELUCTANT_EXPERT.not_this: A simple note of uncertainty that does not function as an authority move

OUTSIDER_VALIDATION.mechanism: Borrows legitimacy from a client, mentor, investor, or outside observer instead of establishing the claim directly.
detection_signals: The message leans on what someone else said about the author or their work
Validation comes from an external party rather than evidence
Named outside approval appears early and shapes the reader's stance
The borrowed endorsement does more work than the underlying substance
OUTSIDER_VALIDATION.example_skeleton: 'A client told me last week that this was the clearest system they had seen, which made me realize...'
OUTSIDER_VALIDATION.not_this: A relevant testimonial used with context and without standing in for the whole argument

PIVOT_NARRATIVE.mechanism: Builds authority through a before-and-after belief shift: I used to think X, now I know Y.
detection_signals: A clean reversal from old belief to new belief
Personal transformation used as proof of insight
The pivot itself is emphasized more than the evidence behind it
The change in view is narrated as a lesson arc
PIVOT_NARRATIVE.example_skeleton: 'I used to think speed mattered most. Now I think clarity matters more than speed.'
PIVOT_NARRATIVE.not_this: A belief update that is carefully supported and not used as the main authority signal

STORYSELLING.mechanism: Disguising a product pitch or lead-generation funnel as a personal diary entry or authentic moment of reflection.
detection_signals: Reads like a personal anecdote but the moral conveniently aligns with the author's offering
Emotional narrative arc that ends at a product, service, or funnel entry point
The 'story' would not exist without the commercial intent behind it
Often uses present tense or 'just happened' framing to feel spontaneous
STORYSELLING.example_skeleton: 'My daughter asked me why I work so much. That conversation changed everything. It is why I built a system to [product pitch]...'
STORYSELLING.not_this: Talking about your work in a way that naturally mentions what you do

persuasion_techniques.description: Common persuasive moves used to make a claim feel urgent, credible, emotional, or socially validated. These sit between broad frameworks and sentence-level phrasing.

LOADED_LANGUAGE.mechanism: Uses emotionally charged wording to push the reader toward a judgment before the argument has fully earned it.
detection_signals: Emotionally heavy words where neutral wording would be possible
Hero-villain framing or moral labeling doing more work than evidence
Adjectives chosen to intensify reaction rather than clarify facts
Language that makes disagreement feel suspect before the case is made
LOADED_LANGUAGE.example_skeleton: 'This broken, outdated approach is killing your growth.'
LOADED_LANGUAGE.not_this: Strong wording that is proportionate to clearly supported facts

APPEAL_TO_AUTHORITY.mechanism: Borrows credibility from titles, institutions, or well-known names instead of building the case mainly on the merits.
detection_signals: Credential-first persuasion: experts, founders, leaders, professors
Institutional prestige used as a substitute for explanation
Named authority invoked without showing why their view settles the matter
Brand or title doing more persuasive work than evidence
APPEAL_TO_AUTHORITY.example_skeleton: 'Three Fortune 500 leaders use this method, so it is the right way to hire.'
APPEAL_TO_AUTHORITY.not_this: Citing relevant expertise while also presenting evidence, limits, and reasoning

APPEAL_TO_FEAR.mechanism: Pushes action by emphasizing threat, loss, or downside more heavily than the underlying reasoning warrants.
detection_signals: Warnings designed to trigger avoidance or panic
Phrases like 'if you keep doing this' tied to severe negative outcomes
Loss-heavy framing with little calibration or nuance
Urgency built primarily on fear of falling behind or getting hurt
APPEAL_TO_FEAR.example_skeleton: 'If you keep writing posts this way, your audience will disappear.'
APPEAL_TO_FEAR.not_this: Explaining a real risk in proportion to the evidence

SOCIAL_PROOF.mechanism: Uses crowd behavior or peer adoption to imply that something is correct, desirable, or safe.
detection_signals: Claims that many people, teams, or creators already do this
Popularity positioned as a reason to comply
Peer adoption used to reduce the need for direct argument
Reader nudged to conform because others supposedly already have
SOCIAL_PROOF.example_skeleton: 'More than 10,000 founders have already switched to this approach.'
SOCIAL_PROOF.not_this: Relevant adoption data that supports but does not replace the main argument

rhetorical_devices.description: Linguistic tricks and structural patterns that make the persuasion feel invisible. These are the connective tissue — they hold the frameworks and tropes together.

CURIOSITY_GAP.mechanism: Withholding a key piece of information to force the reader past the fold ('See more' button) or to keep reading.
detection_signals: Phrases like 'here is why,' 'let me explain,' 'but there is a catch,' 'what happened next changed everything'
The first 2-3 lines promise a revelation that is delayed
Information that could be stated upfront is deliberately withheld for dramatic effect
Often placed right before the LinkedIn 'See more' truncation point

SPECIFICITY_THEATER.mechanism: Using highly specific numbers, timelines, or metrics to create an aura of credibility, even when the specifics are not central to the point.
detection_signals: Suspiciously round or dramatic numbers: '$147K mistake,' '10,000 hours,' '47 rejections'
Metrics that sound precise but are unverifiable
Numbers used primarily for emotional impact rather than informational value
Removing the specific number would not change the actual lesson

MORAL_COMPRESSION.mechanism: Reducing a complex, nuanced situation into a clean, portable lesson or aphorism. The messiness that makes real experience valuable is stripped out in favor of shareability.
detection_signals: Complex situations reduced to a single 'takeaway'
Phrases like 'the lesson is simple' applied to things that are not simple
Real tradeoffs, context-dependence, or ambiguity are erased
The 'insight' could apply to almost anything — it is not specific to the situation described

SAFE_CONTRARIANISM.mechanism: Presenting an opinion as bold or controversial when it is actually widely agreeable, especially to the target audience.
detection_signals: Framed as 'unpopular opinion' or 'hot take' or 'this might get me in trouble'
The opinion would be enthusiastically agreed with by 80%+ of the author's audience
No actual professional or reputational risk to stating it
The 'controversy' is against a vague out-group (recruiters, corporations, academia) rather than the author's own tribe

SEMANTIC_HEDGING.mechanism: Uses soft qualifiers to make a claim feel safer, harder to challenge, or more defensible without really clarifying it.
detection_signals: Heavy use of words like 'might,' 'could,' 'some would say,' or 'in many cases'
Claim is softened just enough to become slippery
Hedging reduces accountability more than it adds precision
The wording makes a weak claim hard to falsify

CALLBACK_CLOSURE.mechanism: Returns to an opening image, phrase, or scene at the end to create emotional neatness and a stronger sense of resolution.
detection_signals: An opening motif reappears near the ending
The closing line echoes the beginning for rhetorical neatness
Structure creates a satisfying loop around a thin core idea
The symmetry makes the draft feel more complete than the substance alone would

RULE_OF_THREE_PADDING.mechanism: Uses a polished three-part list or tricolon to make a simple point feel fuller, more memorable, or more complete than it really is.
detection_signals: Three-part phrasing used for cadence more than clarity
Tidy triples like 'clarity, consistency, courage'
List structure adds rhetorical weight to a thin idea
The symmetry is memorable even when the content is light

logical_fallacies.description: Reasoning shortcuts that make an argument feel cleaner, stronger, or simpler than it really is. These matter when the structure of the claim distorts the substance.

FALSE_DILEMMA.mechanism: Presents two options as if they are the only possibilities, even when the real situation allows more nuance or middle ground.
detection_signals: Binary framing: either X or Y
Complex issue reduced to a forced choice
Missing middle positions, tradeoffs, or alternatives
Language that treats one preferred option as the only sane one
FALSE_DILEMMA.example_skeleton: 'Either you build a personal brand or you become invisible.'
FALSE_DILEMMA.not_this: A real two-option constraint where alternatives are genuinely absent

HASTY_GENERALIZATION.mechanism: Draws a broad conclusion from a small sample, a few anecdotes, or a narrow personal experience.
detection_signals: Big rule inferred from one or two examples
Personal anecdote treated as universal evidence
Claims about 'people,' 'customers,' or 'the market' with little support
A small pattern stretched into a general law
HASTY_GENERALIZATION.example_skeleton: 'I sent two cold emails and both failed, so cold email is dead.'
HASTY_GENERALIZATION.not_this: A tentative observation that clearly states its limits

CAUSAL_OVERSIMPLIFICATION.mechanism: Explains a complex result with one tidy cause, removing competing explanations and real-world messiness.
detection_signals: Single-cause explanation for a multi-factor outcome
Clean 'the reason is simple' framing on a messy topic
Ignored context, incentives, timing, or second-order effects
Cause-and-effect language that feels too neat for the situation
CAUSAL_OVERSIMPLIFICATION.example_skeleton: 'This product failed because the founder did not post on LinkedIn enough.'
CAUSAL_OVERSIMPLIFICATION.not_this: A focused causal claim that acknowledges limits and other contributing factors

CHERRY_PICKING.mechanism: Selects only the examples, metrics, or facts that support the preferred conclusion while leaving out the balancing evidence.
detection_signals: Only favorable examples are highlighted
Metrics shown without the surrounding context
Counterexamples or caveats quietly disappear
The chosen evidence feels curated to prove a point rather than test it
CHERRY_PICKING.example_skeleton: 'These three viral posts prove this strategy always works.'
CHERRY_PICKING.not_this: Selective examples that are clearly labeled as illustrative rather than decisive

cognitive_biases.description: Audience-level judgment shortcuts that persuasive writing often leans on. These are not always deliberate, but they help explain why some framing lands so easily.

CONFIRMATION_BIAS.mechanism: Leans into what the audience already believes or wants to believe, making agreement feel natural and frictionless.
detection_signals: Flatters the reader's prior worldview
Frames an existing belief as newly validated
Uses familiar grievances or assumptions as the foundation
Presents agreement as obvious because the audience already leans that way
CONFIRMATION_BIAS.example_skeleton: 'Deep down, you already know most career advice online is fake.'
CONFIRMATION_BIAS.not_this: Meeting the reader where they are while still challenging weak assumptions

LOSS_AVERSION.mechanism: Makes potential losses feel heavier and more motivating than equivalent gains.
detection_signals: Emphasis on what the reader will lose by not acting
Downside language outweighs upside language
Risk of missing out framed as more important than possible benefit
Reader pushed by fear of decline rather than interest in improvement
LOSS_AVERSION.example_skeleton: 'If you ignore this now, you will keep wasting months and momentum.'
LOSS_AVERSION.not_this: Balanced discussion of costs and benefits

HALO_EFFECT.mechanism: Lets one admired trait, credential, or success spill over and make unrelated claims feel more credible.
detection_signals: One success or credential used to support a broader claim
Admiration for the speaker carries the argument
Readers are nudged to trust the message because the messenger seems impressive
Status or charisma substitutes for topic-specific support
HALO_EFFECT.example_skeleton: 'She built a unicorn, so her framework for writing cold emails must be right.'
HALO_EFFECT.not_this: Relevant expertise used carefully and within scope

ANCHORING.mechanism: Makes the first number, frame, or comparison point do disproportionate work in shaping later judgment.
detection_signals: A big first number or baseline sets expectations
Opening comparison point makes the rest seem reasonable
Early framing narrows what feels normal or acceptable
The first claim keeps influencing the reader even when later nuance appears
ANCHORING.example_skeleton: 'Most teams waste six figures on this before they realize the simple fix.'
ANCHORING.not_this: Using a starting reference point that is clearly contextualized and not over-weighted

platform_tactics.description: Formatting, engagement, and pressure patterns designed to exploit feed behavior, inbox dynamics, or conversion psychology. These are not just about what the draft says — they are also about how it is packaged to trigger action.

BROETRY.mechanism: One sentence per line, heavy use of white space, designed to increase vertical scroll distance and dwell time — metrics most social platform algorithms reward.
detection_signals: One sentence (or sentence fragment) per line
Excessive line breaks between thoughts that could be a normal paragraph
Short, punchy lines that read like dramatic pauses
The formatting would look absurd in any context other than a social feed

ENGAGEMENT_FARMING.mechanism: Appending a generic question or call for interaction solely to trigger comments, which boosts algorithmic distribution.
detection_signals: Question at the end that is loosely connected (or unconnected) to the post's content
Broad questions designed to be easy to answer: 'What is your biggest challenge?', 'Agree?'
The question does not reflect genuine curiosity — the author is unlikely to read the answers
Phrases like 'drop a [emoji] if you agree', 'tag someone who needs this'

DISGUISED_CTA.mechanism: Embedding a lead-generation or sales action inside language that sounds like peer conversation rather than marketing.
detection_signals: Phrases like 'DM me [keyword]' or 'comment [word] and I will send you...'
Offers framed as personal favors: 'I put together a free guide, happy to share'
The 'generosity' routes to an email list, sales funnel, or consultation booking
What sounds like sharing is actually a conversion mechanism

FAKE_SCARCITY.mechanism: Creates pressure by implying limited supply, access, or opportunity when the limitation is weak, artificial, or unverifiable.
detection_signals: Claims like 'only a few spots left' without context
Scarcity framing that cannot be checked
Availability pressure doing more work than the actual offer
The message wants urgency because something seems rare rather than useful

ARTIFICIAL_URGENCY.mechanism: Pushes immediate action through countdown-style time pressure that feels manufactured rather than genuinely necessary.
detection_signals: Last chance, today only, final hours, closing tonight
Time pressure with no clear reason behind the deadline
Urgency language used to suppress reflection
The reader is pushed to act now rather than think clearly

CONFIRMSHAMING.mechanism: Frames non-compliance as laziness, ignorance, or self-sabotage so that saying no feels embarrassing.
detection_signals: Declining is framed as a failure of ambition or intelligence
The negative option is worded to make the reader feel small
Opting out is treated as an admission of weakness
Social discomfort is used as conversion pressure

FAKE_PERSONALIZATION.mechanism: Uses a personalized-sounding opener to create warmth or relevance before moving into a generic or templated pitch.
detection_signals: Opens with 'came across your work' or a similar soft compliment
The personalized line is vague and could fit many recipients
The message quickly pivots into a generic ask or pitch
Apparent familiarity does more work than actual relevance

NAMEDROP_OPENER.mechanism: Leads with a prestigious person, company, investor, or shared contact to borrow credibility before the real message begins.
detection_signals: Opening line mentions a notable person, company, or shared connection
Prestige appears before the core point is made
The namedrop is used to soften skepticism or speed trust
The borrowed association feels more important than the actual ask

REPLY_CHAIN_DECEPTION.mechanism: Formats a cold message so it looks like part of an existing thread or prior relationship, lowering the reader's defenses.
detection_signals: Subject or opener implies a prior exchange that did not happen
Message is formatted to resemble an ongoing thread
The draft tries to create false familiarity through continuity cues
Reader is nudged to treat a cold message as already-established context

GRATITUDE_THEATER.mechanism: Uses public thanks, shoutouts, or appreciation language partly as a visibility or engagement move rather than mainly as genuine acknowledgment.
detection_signals: Thanks or praise feels performative or strategically public
The gratitude section mainly boosts visibility, affiliation, or social proof
Named appreciation sits awkwardly close to self-positioning
The acknowledgment does more platform work than relational work

NEWSLETTER_BAIT.mechanism: Ends otherwise unrelated content with a repeated subscription nudge that turns the whole draft toward list growth.
detection_signals: Post closes with a newsletter or subscribe push regardless of topic fit
The main content feels partially instrumental to list growth
A recurring opt-in prompt appears as standard packaging
Subscription language arrives even when the draft would stand fine without it

TRANSFORMATION_SNAPSHOT.mechanism: Compresses a long, messy process into a simple before-and-after frame to make change look clean, fast, and highly legible.
detection_signals: Before/after framing removes the messy middle
A process is flattened into two tidy states
Transformation is shown as a snapshot rather than a gradual path
The clean contrast makes the outcome feel more dramatic and portable
